text: Chapter 14

During that first week, the wisteria began to fade, and the petals from the Judas and peach trees fell, carpeting the ground in rose-pink. Soon all the freesias disappeared, and the irises became rare. As these flowers faded, the yellow banksia roses bloomed, and the large summer roses suddenly burst into color along the walls and trellises. Among them was Fortune's Yellow, a stunning rose. Soon the tamarisk and daphne bushes were at their peak, and the lilies grew to their full height. By the end of the week, the fig trees were providing shade, plum blossoms appeared among the olive trees, the modest pink shrubs bloomed, and thick-leaved, star-shaped flowers sprawled over the rocks in bright purple and pale lemon-yellow.

By the end of the week, Mister Wilkins arrived, just as his wife had predicted. He had seemed almost eager to accept her invitation, since he hadn't even waited to write back and had sent a telegram instead.

That was definitely eager. Scrap thought it showed a real desire to reunite. Watching Lotty's happy face and knowing how much she wanted Mellersh to enjoy his vacation, Scrap thought he would be an absolute fool to waste his time paying attention to anyone else. If he isn't nice to her, Scrap thought, we should take him to the edge of the terrace and throw him off. By the end of the week, she and Missus Wilkins were calling each other Caroline and Lotty, and had become close friends.

Missus Wilkins had always behaved like a friend, though Scrap had tried not to. She had tried to be careful, but being cautious around Missus Wilkins was impossible. She was completely free of reservations and so open that soon Scrap, almost without realizing it, found herself being open too. And no one could be more open than Scrap once she relaxed.

The only problem with Lotty was that she was almost always somewhere else. You couldn't catch her or sit her down for a chat. Scrap's earlier fear that she would be clingy seemed ridiculous now. She wasn't clingy at all. Dinner and the evenings were the only times you actually saw her. She was invisible all day, returning in the late afternoon looking like a mess, with bits of moss in her hair and her freckles darker than ever. Maybe she was trying to do everything she wanted before Mellersh arrived, intending to spend her time with him later, looking neat and wearing her best clothes.

Scrap watched her, fascinated despite herself, because it seemed amazing that anyone could be so happy with so little. San Salvatore was beautiful and the weather was perfect, but scenery and weather had never been enough for Scrap. How could they be enough for someone who would soon have to leave and go back to Hampstead? Plus, Mellersh was arriving—the very Mellersh Lotty had just run away from. It was nice to think you should share and make a grand gesture, but the grand gestures Scrap knew of had never made anyone happy. No one liked being the recipient of charity, and it always took effort from the person making the gesture. Yet she had to admit Lotty showed no effort at all; it was clear that everything she said and did was completely natural, and that she was just purely, simply happy.

And Lotty really was happy. By the middle of the week, her doubts about whether she could stay calm and peaceful around Mellersh all day had vanished. She felt completely unshakable. She was ready for anything, rooted firmly in paradise. Whatever Mellersh said or did, she wouldn't leave her state of bliss or allow herself to get angry for even a second. Instead, she was going to bring him up into this happy state with her. They would sit together in the warmth and laugh about how afraid of him she used to be in Hampstead, and how that fear had made her lie to him. And he wouldn't need much persuading. He would adjust naturally after a day or two, carried along by the sweet breezes of this perfect place. There he would sit, covered in stars, thought Missus Wilkins, whose mind occasionally drifted to poetic thoughts. She laughed to herself at the image of Mellersh—a serious, formal lawyer wearing a top hat and black coat—covered in stars. But it was an affectionate laugh, full of pride in how good he would look. “Poor guy,” she murmured to herself warmly. “What he needs is to air out a bit.”

This was during the first half of the week. By the second half, right before Mister Wilkins arrived, she stopped telling herself that she was unshakable or that the atmosphere had changed her. She didn't even think about it anymore; she just took it for granted. As she put it, both to herself and to Lady Caroline, she had found her footing in paradise.

Against Missus Fisher's ideas of proper etiquette—which was typical of Missus Wilkins—she didn't go to meet her husband at the train station in Mezzago. Instead, she just walked down to the street in Castagneto where Beppo's carriage would drop him and his bags. Missus Fisher wasn't happy about Mister Wilkins's arrival and was sure that anyone married to Missus Wilkins must be a bit foolish. Still, she believed a husband should always be met properly. She had always met Mister Fisher. Never once in their marriage had he arrived at a station without her there, and she always saw him off too. These polite habits strengthened a marriage, making a husband feel he could count on his wife always being there. Always being there was the key secret for a wife. She preferred not to think about what would have happened to Mister Fisher if she had ignored this rule. Enough things happened to him as it was; no matter how careful you were, marriage always had its issues.

But Missus Wilkins didn't worry about any of that. She just walked down the hill singing—Missus Fisher could hear her—and met her husband in the street as casually as if she were picking up a dropped pin. The other three women, who were still in bed since it was early, heard her pass beneath their windows on her way to meet Mister Wilkins's morning train. Scrap smiled, Rose sighed, and Missus Fisher rang her bell to ask Francesca to bring breakfast to her room. All three of them decided to eat breakfast in their rooms that day, sharing a natural instinct to hide.

Scrap always had breakfast in bed, but she felt the same urge to stay hidden, so she planned to spend the whole day in her room. However, she realized she might not need to hide as much today as tomorrow. Today, she calculated, Mellersh would be busy. He would want a bath, and taking a hot bath at San Salvatore was a major project that took a lot of time. It required the help of the entire staff. Domenico and the young helper Giuseppe had to coax the complicated stove to burn, keeping it from burning too hot, blowing on it when it started to die, and relighting it when it went out. Francesca had to watch the tap closely to control the flow; if it was turned on too much, the water went cold, and if not enough, the stove exploded inside and flooded the house. Meanwhile, Costanza and Angela ran back and forth carrying buckets of hot water from the kitchen to help.

The tub had been installed recently and was both the pride and the terror of the staff. It was a modern patent, and nobody really understood how it worked. Long instructions were printed on the wall, filled with the word pericoloso—dangerous. When Missus Fisher saw that word on her first day, she immediately returned to her room and ordered a basin of water instead. When the others realized what using the bath involved—how the servants refused to leave them alone with the stove, how Francesca insisted on staying with her back turned to watch the tap, and how the rest of the staff waited outside the door until they came out safely—they also chose to have basins of water brought to their rooms.

Mister Wilkins, however, was a man and would surely want a proper bath. Scrap figured this would keep him occupied for a long time. Then he would unpack, and after traveling all night, he would probably sleep until evening. He would be busy all day and wouldn't be around until dinner.

So Scrap decided she would be safe in the garden after all. She got up, dressed slowly, and listened to the sounds of Mister Wilkins's arrival. She heard his bags being carried into Lotty's room across the hall, and heard his refined voice ask, “Do I tip this fellow?” followed by, “Can I have a hot bath?” Lotty's voice cheerfully replied that he didn't need to tip the man because he was their gardener, and that yes, he could have a hot bath. Soon, the hallway was filled with the usual noises of wood and water being carried, running feet, and shouting voices as the bath was prepared.

Scrap finished dressing and waited by her window, listening for Mister Wilkins to enter the bathroom. Once he was safely inside, she would slip out to the garden and continue thinking about the meaning of her life. She was making progress. She was sleeping less and starting to agree that 'superficial' was the right word for her past. She also worried that her future looked bleak.
There—she heard Mister Wilkins's voice again. Lotty's door opened, and he came out, asking for directions to the bathroom.
“It's where you see the crowd,” Lotty replied—still sounding cheerful, Scrap was glad to hear.

His footsteps moved down the hall while Lotty went downstairs. Then there was a brief argument at the bathroom door—or rather, a chorus of shouting from the servants and a quiet determination from Mister Wilkins to bathe alone.

Mister Wilkins didn't speak Italian, and the warning pericoloso meant nothing to him—even if he had noticed the sign on the wall, which he hadn't. He shut the door firmly in the servants' faces, pushing back Domenico, who tried to follow him in. He locked himself in, thinking about how strange it was that these foreigners, both men and women, wanted to watch him bathe. He had heard that in Finland, local women actually helped wash travelers in the bath. But he hadn't heard of that happening in Italy, which seemed much more civilized—probably because people actually vacationed here, unlike Finland.

Thinking this over and comparing the civilizations of Italy and Finland, Mister Wilkins got into the tub and turned off the tap. Naturally, he shut it off, as anyone would. But the red instructions on the wall specifically said the tap must stay open as long as there was fire in the stove. It had to trickle until the fire was completely out; otherwise—and here was that word pericoloso again—the stove would explode.

Mister Wilkins got in, shut off the tap, and the stove exploded just as the instructions warned. Fortunately, it only blew up internally, but it made a massive noise. Mister Wilkins jumped out of the tub and ran to the door, grabbing a towel on his way out only out of pure habit.
Scrap, who was halfway across the hall on her way outside, heard the blast.
Good grief, she thought, remembering the warnings. There goes Mister Wilkins!
She ran toward the stairs to call the servants, just as Mister Wilkins ran out clutching his towel, and they collided.
“That damn bath!” Mister Wilkins shouted, losing his temper for probably the first time in his life; he was very shaken.

What an introduction. Mister Wilkins, barely covered by a towel, with his bare shoulders at one end and his legs at the other, meeting Lady Caroline Dester—the very woman he had swallowed his pride to come to Italy to see.

Lotty had mentioned in her letter who was staying at the castle, and Mister Wilkins had immediately realized this was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Lotty had simply written, “There are two other women here, Missus Fisher and Lady Caroline Dester,” but that was plenty. He knew all about her wealthy, influential family and their historical connections. He knew they could easily hire another lawyer if they wanted to, and they had many legal affairs that needed managing. He had also heard about the famous beauty of their daughter. Even if the parents didn't need a lawyer, their daughter might, since beautiful women often found themselves in complicated situations. And even if none of them ever hired him, knowing them was still incredibly valuable. It opened doors and offered endless possibilities. He could live in Hampstead for the rest of his life and never get another chance like this.

As soon as he got his wife's letter, he telegraphed and packed his bags. This was business, and he didn't waste time when it came to business. He also knew it was important to be friendly. He had greeted his wife warmly, knowing that being nice was the smart thing to do. In fact, he actually felt very happy because for once, Lotty was helping his career. He had kissed her when he got out of the carriage, thanked her for waking up early, and didn't complain about the steep walk up to the castle. He talked pleasantly about his trip and admired the views when she pointed them out. He had his whole day planned: shave, bathe, change, take a nap, and then meet Lady Caroline at lunch.

On the train, he had carefully chosen his introductory words, practicing how he would politely express his pleasure in meeting her, referencing her famous family and her brother's war medal with perfect tact. He felt this meeting could be the turning point of his career.

And now look at him... it was horrific. What could be worse? He was wearing nothing but a towel, with water dripping down his legs, and he had just sworn. He knew instantly the woman was Lady Caroline. Mister Wilkins rarely swore, and never in front of a lady or a client. And the towel! Why had he come here? He should have stayed in Hampstead. He would never live this down.
But Scrap surprised him. Although she had to squeeze her face to keep from laughing, she managed to control herself and said as calmly as if he were fully dressed, “How do you do.”
What amazing manners. Mister Wilkins could have worshipped her. She completely ignored the towel. That was true high-class behavior.

Full of gratitude, he shook her hand and replied, “How do you do.” Saying the normal words made everything feel normal again. He was so relieved that he forgot he was only wearing a towel and fell back into his professional routine. He forgot what he looked like, but he didn't forget who she was, or that he had just sworn in front of her. He had to apologize immediately. Swearing in front of a lady—and this lady of all people—was awful.
“I am afraid I used terrible language,” Mister Wilkins said, speaking as formally as if he were wearing a suit.
“I thought it was very appropriate,” Scrap said, since she was used to hearing people swear.
Mister Wilkins was incredibly relieved. She wasn't offended. Only someone from a truly noble family could be so relaxed and understanding.
“I am speaking to Lady Caroline Dester, correct?” he asked, making his voice sound as polished as possible to hide his massive relief.

“Yes,” Scrap said, and she couldn't help but smile. She hadn't planned to smile at Mister Wilkins, ever, but he looked so ridiculous standing there in a towel, completely ignoring his bare legs while talking like a priest.
“Allow me to introduce myself,” Mister Wilkins said with formal politeness. “My name is Mellersh-Wilkins.”
He instinctively offered his hand a second time.
“I thought so,” Scrap said, shaking his hand again, unable to stop smiling.

He was about to start one of the compliments he had practiced on the train, completely forgetting he was naked, when the servants ran up the stairs and Missus Fisher appeared in her doorway. The explosion had happened fast, and the servants in the kitchen and Missus Fisher outside hadn't had time to arrive until now.

The servants knew exactly what the noise meant and ran straight to the bathroom to stop the water, ignoring the man in the towel. But Missus Fisher had no idea what the noise was and froze in her doorway.
It was a shocking sight. Lady Caroline was shaking hands with a man who was clearly Missus Wilkins's husband in a towel, and they were chatting as if nothing was wrong.
Scrap noticed Missus Fisher and turned to her. “Let me introduce Mister Mellersh-Wilkins,” she said smoothly. “He just arrived. Mister Wilkins, this is Missus Fisher.”
And Mister Wilkins, always polite, responded immediately. He bowed to the elderly lady, walked over to her, leaving wet footprints on the floor, and offered his hand.
“It is a pleasure to meet a friend of my wife's,” Mister Wilkins said in his refined voice.
Scrap quietly slipped away down to the garden.
